summary: POC scoping call to define latency/throughput SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), sizing, and benchmark plan. Customer needs p95/p99 targets for both time-to-first-token and time-per-token across conversational and batch workloads. Agreement to run two benchmark phases: synthetic replay of prod traces and closed-loop end-to-end tests on Dedicated nodes.
topics: POC goals; current stack & constraints; TTFT vs TPOT definitions; p95/p99 targets; workload sizing (seq len, concurrency); measurement plan (where to instrument, artifacts); timeline and next steps
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-07-27 15:00 PDT | Duration: 48m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE) -- Michael Torres (Orion CTO), Priya Singh (Orion ML Eng), Daniel Park (Orion Infra), Sara Gomez (Orion PM)
Recording URL: https://redwood-recordings.s3/ff-20270727-orion-001 (internal)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we were gonna run through the POC scope for latency and throughput SL- SLOs. I know you sent over the doc Sara, so thanks for that.
[00:20] Michael Torres: Yeah thanks, Alex. Our main ask is we need strong guarantees for TTFT and also steady TPOT under load, basically p95 and p99 targets for both. We're evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted but leaning Dedicated for isolation.
[00:35] Priya Rao: Great, just to align the defs early, when we say TTFT we mean time to first token from request accept, and TPOT is time per output token for the streaming phase, right?
[00:50] Priya Singh: Correct, TTFT is our main customer-facing metric for interactive chat. For batch inference TPOT matters more for total throughput.
[01:05] Jordan Lee: Quick note, sometimes folks call TPOT "time per token" or per-token latency, and some infra folks measure tokens/sec instead. We'll make sure to include both conversions in the benchmark sheet.
[01:25] Sara Gomez: Our target ballpark: p95 TTFT <= 120ms and p99 TTFT <= 220ms for short convs (~16-64 tokens). For longer responses average token throughput should keep p95 TPOT <= 12ms/token, p99 <= 25ms/token. Those are aspirational.
[01:48] Alex Chen: Got it, that's helpful. Can I ask about your current stack and typical seq lengths and concurrency?
[02:00] Michael Torres: We're on GCP, model serving today is a mix of Vertex endpoints and some in-house Triton-based infra. Typical conversational seq len: prompt ~48 tokens, response ~64 tokens. Peak QPS per endpoint ~120 req/s, sustained ~40qps. Concurrency spikes up to 600 concurrent open connections during business hours.
[02:30] Priya Rao: Ok that suggests we need to size for both steady-state and burst. For Dedicated we recommend starting with 4x A100-equivalent GPUs for baseline and run autoscale tests. We'll tune batch sizes; small batch for TTFT, larger for TPOT.
[02:50] Daniel Park: We have strict network egress and VPC peering rules; if we do Private deployment, need to ensure KMS integration and audit logs. Also, can we run the benchmarks inside our staging VPC?
[03:05] Jordan Lee: Yes, we can. We'll set up a staging cluster with private control plane and run the replay tests there. For security we will share SOC2 and network diagrams.
[03:22] Michael Torres: On measurement approach, we want two metrics sets: user-facing (measured at gateway) and infra-level (measured at model container). The delta is helpful to capture network & routing overhead.
[03:37] Alex Chen: Agreed. Our plan: instrument at three points: client gateway (TTFT measured at request edge), Redwood ingress (when request arrives at runtime), and model token emit time (runtime trace). We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and also tokens/sec curves.
[04:00] Priya Singh: Can you record exact definitions in the benchmark sheet? We need clear formulas: TTFT = t_first_token - t_request_received_at_edge, TPOT = average(t_token_i - t_token_{i-1}) over token stream, plus tail percentiles.
[04:20] Alex Chen: Yes we'll put formulas and example queries. Also we'll include synthetic microbenchmarks (single request repeated), replay of production traces, and end-to-end UX tests with streaming clients.
[04:36] Sara Gomez: For replay, we can sanitize and provide 2 hours of traces. Priya (Orion) will export.
[04:45] Priya Singh: Yup I'll pull traces, but keep in mind the traces have a mix of short answers and long explanations. We'll tag by response length.
[05:00] Jordan Lee: Important to note: TTFT is very sensitive to batching and cold starts. We'll run warm-up ramps and continuous traffic to avoid cold-start artifacts in final results.
[05:14] Michael Torres: Cold starts are a big no for us; we need steady-state guarantees after a 5-minute warm-up. Also can you measure p99 during traffic spikes?
[05:28] Priya Rao: We'll include spike tests: sudden 3x QPS for 2 minutes, sustained then back to baseline, and measure p95/p99 across phases.
[05:40] Alex Chen: On tooling, we suggest using our benchmark harness (we'll share link) which can replay at exact QPS, maintain concurrency, and collect token timestamps. It instruments HTTP hooks and optionally gRPC.
[05:54] Priya Singh: Are you able to simulate network overhead similar to our prod egress? We see about 15ms average network hop to model infra.
[06:05] Jordan Lee: Yes we can add artificial latency in the replay to approximate that. We'll also run tests colocated to measure best-case.
[06:18] Michael Torres: How do you handle quantized models and TPOT variance? We plan to try int8 quant and FP16.
[06:30] Alex Chen: We'll include model variants in the catalog. For TPOT we expect quantized profiles to reduce per-token time but may increase variance. We'll run multiple seeds and report median and tail stats.
[06:45] Sara Gomez: What's your recommended logging cadence for metrics? We want to ingest into Datadog.
[06:55] Priya Rao: We'll produce time-series with 1s granularity for gateway, and 100ms buckets for infra traces. We'll export CSVs and a JSON trace bundle that you can ingest.
[07:10] Priya Singh: About SLOs, are you recommending separate SLOs for TTFT and TPOT or a combined SLO? We think separate makes sense.
[07:20] Alex Chen: We recommend separate SLOs with alerting tied to the user-facing metric (edge TTFT) and infra SLOs to trigger autoscale or fallback. For example, if infra TPOT p99 > 30ms for >5 minutes, trigger scale-up or fallback to cheaper model.
[07:38] Michael Torres: For fallback, can Redwood automatically route to a faster smaller model if TPOT spikes? We want graceful degradation.
[07:48] Jordan Lee: Yes, routing policies support automatic fallback to compatible model variants and region-based failover. We'll demo that in the dedicated POC.
[07:58] Sara Gomez: Timeline check, we want results in 3 weeks. Is that feasible?
[08:05] Alex Chen: Rough plan: Week 1: ingest traces and configure test env; Week 2: run replay synthetic + ramp tests; Week 3: run end-to-end UX tests, compile results and recommendations. So 3 weeks is tight but doable if we get traces and access quickly.
[08:24] Daniel Park: Access note: we'll need a service account and peering info. I'll coordinate with your infra.
[08:33] Priya Rao: We'll provide a runbook for access steps. Also a note on measurements: TTFT measured at edge should exclude queue time in API gateway if you have separate queueing; we will call out queue vs processing latency.
[08:50] Priya Singh: For batch workloads (nightly embeddings), our SLOs are different; we want throughput targets: tokens/sec and cost per 1M tokens. Can you include cost modeling?
[09:03] Alex Chen: Yes Redwood Optimize can output cost-performance tradeoffs for batch. We'll include sample calculations in the spreadsheet and run a cost experiment for the batch pipeline.
[09:15] Michael Torres: One more ask: include p99 across both TTFT and TPOT for the 95th-99th percentile during sustained traffic and during spikes.
[09:28] Jordan Lee: We'll include per-phase percentiles and a breakdown by request type (short/medium/long).
[09:36] Sara Gomez: For documentation, please add the exact endpoints you'll hit, payload samples, and environment variables so our infra can open ports.
[09:47] Alex Chen: Will do. We'll also include a small acceptance criteria doc: e.g. "POC passes if TTFT p95 <= 120ms and p99 <= 220ms for short convs, and TPOT p95 <= 12ms and p99 <= 25ms for long responses across steady-state and spike tests".
[10:08] Priya Singh: If we fall short, we want remediation steps: tuning batch sizes, changing kernel selection, or fallback routing to a lower-latency model.
[10:20] Alex Chen: Exactly. We'll include recommended tuning knobs and expected unit impacts.
[10:28] Michael Torres: Any concerns around measurement noise? We want repeatability.
[10:34] Priya Rao: We'll run multiple iterations, use warm-up, and report confidence intervals. We'll also provide raw traces so you can recompute percentiles.
[10:45] Daniel Park: For the Dedicated infra do you have SLA numbers? We need to compare to our internal SLAs.
[10:52] Jordan Lee: Dedicated offers SLA-backed latency targets for specific instance sizes; we'll share the SLA doc. However SLOs in POC are really driven by workload and tuning.
[11:05] Sara Gomez: Okay quick recap, please list the immediate deliverables.
[11:10] Alex Chen: Recap: 1) Redwood to share benchmark config sheet + harness link (Alex); 2) Orion to share sanitized traces and QPS profiles (Priya); 3) Redwood SE to provision staging Dedicated cluster and run baseline tests (Jordan); 4) Security docs (SOC2, network diagrams) to be shared (Alex).
[11:30] Priya Singh: Timeline notes: Priya will try to get traces by Aug 2, Alex will schedule test run for week of Aug 9.
[11:40] Michael Torres: Sounds good. We also want a short executive summary after tests to share with the leadership.
[11:48] Alex Chen: We'll deliver an executive summary with charts and recommended next steps.
[12:00] Sara Gomez: Thanks all, let's reconvene after baseline tests.
[12:05] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone, talk soon.

End of transcript.
